title: Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over IEEE 802 Networks
summary: Specifies a standard way to carry IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies over IEEE 802 networks, so that implementations are compatible and interoperable. It was an Internet standard and replaces RFC 948.

eli5.summary: It tells how to put Internet packets into the envelopes that local office networks use, so different brands of equipment understand each other.

questions: how are ip datagrams sent over ieee 802
what is ip encapsulation on ieee 802 networks
what is the mtu for ieee 802.3 networks
subtitle: The standard recipe for carrying IP datagrams and ARP over Ethernet-style IEEE 802 LANs.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802 LANs (802.3, 802.4 and 802.5) differ from each other, so equipment from different makers needed one agreed way to carry IP and ARP.
tldr.mechanism: IP datagrams and ARP packets are wrapped in an 802.2 LLC Type 1 frame with a SNAP header. DSAP and SSAP are 170, control is 3, the organization code is zero, and the EtherType says IP (2048) or ARP (2054). Addresses are resolved with ARP.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that replaces RFC 948 and gives per-network rules for packet sizes, broadcasts and 802.5 source routing.

today: RFC 1042 is an Internet Standard. It replaced RFC 948 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Goal and Scope
sections.content:
The goal is compatible and interoperable implementations for sending IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies over IEEE 802 networks. The memo covers three of them: 802.3, 802.4 and 802.5. It aims to make sure all equipment using IP or ARP on the same type of network will interoperate. It is not required that use be identical across the three types, only within each type.

The IEEE physical layer standards define the physical layer and the Media Access Control sublayer, and 802.2 defines the Logical Link Control (LLC) sublayer. Sometimes the use of IP and ARP has to be limited relative to what an 802 standard allows. The memo does not fully describe interoperation through IEEE 802.1 transparent bridges, pending completion of that standard.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of office networks work a bit differently. This memo makes sure every maker puts internet packets on each kind in the same way.

sections.title: The LLC and SNAP Header
sections.content:
IP datagrams travel inside 802.2 LLC and SNAP, on top of the 802.3, 802.4 or 802.5 MAC layer. LLC and SNAP together are 8 octets. The header holds DSAP=K1, SSAP=K1 and a control byte, then the SNAP fields: an organization code K2 and a 16-bit EtherType.

K1 is 170 (the global SAP value for SNAP), K2 is 0 and the control value is 3 (Unnumbered Information). The EtherType values are 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP. Normally all communication uses 802.2 type 1, which every implementation must support. Consenting systems may use type 2 after checking with XID.
sections.eli5: Every packet gets a small label at the front. It says this is an internet packet and what kind, so the receiving machine knows what to do with it.

sections.title: Address Mapping with ARP
sections.content:
A 32-bit Internet address must be mapped to a 16-bit or 48-bit 802 address by the dynamic ARP procedure. Each host must know its own Internet address, answer ARP requests, and use ARP to translate other hosts' addresses.

The ARP fields are fixed for 802 networks. The hardware type code for IEEE 802 networks of all kinds is 6. The protocol type for IP is 2048. The hardware address length is 2 for 16-bit addresses or 6 for 48-bit addresses, the protocol address length is 4, and the operation code is 1 for a request and 2 for a reply. The broadcast Internet address should map to the all-ones 802 broadcast address.
sections.eli5: To send to a friend you have to know their street address. ARP is shouting, who has this internet number, and the right computer answers with its hardware address.

sections.title: Frame Sizes and Padding
sections.content:
Frames are sent as LLC Type 1 Unnumbered Information with control code 3. When the 802 network has a minimum frame size, the data field should be padded with zero octets. The padding is not part of the IP datagram and is not counted in the IP total length field. The minimum IP packet size used is 28 octets (20 for the IP header plus 8 for LLC and SNAP). The minimum ARP packet is 24 octets, and the typical one is 32.

All hosts on one network must use the same MTU. Gateways must be ready to accept full-length packets and fragment them when necessary. Hosts should accept full-length packets but must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they know the destination accepts them.

The IP datagram limits per network are worked out from the 802 frame limits. For 10BASE5 802.3 the maximum frame is 1518 octets, leaving 1492 for the datagram, which differs from the 1500 octet Ethernet MTU. For 802.4 the maximum is 8191 octets, leaving 8166. For 802.5 with a 9 millisecond token-holding time on a 4 megabit/second ring, it is 4508 octets, leaving 4464. Implementations are recommended to support IP packets of at least 2002 octets on 802.5.
sections.eli5: Each kind of network has a maximum size for a package. The memo does the arithmetic, subtracting the envelope, to find how much internet data fits inside.

sections.title: IEEE 802.5 Source Routing
sections.content:
Many 802.5 token ring implementations add multi-ring source routing through a Routing Information Field (RIF) in the MAC header. The memo describes existing implementations and makes no attempt to specify a future standard. A Routing Information Indicator bit in the source address shows whether a RIF is present.

The RIF has a 2-octet Routing Control field followed by 0 to 8 two-octet route designators. The control field holds 3 broadcast bits (000 non-broadcast, 100 all-routes, 110 single-route), a 5-bit length, a direction bit, a 3-bit largest-frame code and 4 reserved bits. A receiver rejects a frame whose largest-frame value is smaller than its MTU.

For ARP, it is desirable but not required to first send an all-stations broadcast without a RIF, then fall back to an all-routes or single-route broadcast. IP broadcasts must be sent as single-route broadcasts, since multiple copies would harm many protocols. All implementations must understand frames with no RIF or an empty RIF. All IP and ARP packets should be sent at the default 802.5 priority, which is 3.
sections.eli5: On a network of several connected rings, a packet can carry a route map. This part says how to read the map, and how to avoid getting many copies of the same broadcast.

sections.title: Trailers and Ethernet Coexistence
sections.content:
Some Unix 4.x bsd systems use a trailer encapsulation for better performance on the VAX. Consenting systems on the same 802 network may use it between themselves, but all hosts must be able to communicate using the standard non-trailer method.

Ethernet and IEEE 802.3 link protocols can share one physical cable. A computer that reads both must remember which one each peer uses, and link-level broadcasts reach only the computers that use the same protocol. The memo therefore recommends using an IP gateway as if there were two distinct networks. Ethernet allows a 1500 octet IP datagram, while 802.3 allows only 1492.
sections.eli5: Two kinds of network languages can share a single cable, but a broadcast in one language is not heard by speakers of the other. The safe fix is to treat them as two separate networks.
